newsitem.title: GERMANY: German "pilot" pay deal in metal sector fails.
newsitem.headline: German "pilot" pay deal in metal sector fails.

text.p: Regional talks between the IG Metall engineering union and employers in the state of Baden-Wuertemberg aimed at securing a deal on wages and labour costs in the sector collapsed on Friday, the two sides said.

There had been hopes that a deal in the south-west state could then have been used as a "pilot" agreement in other regions to solve a bitter dispute over proposed cuts to sick pay entitlements and other benefits.

But IG Metall leaders said after the 19-hour talks broke down early on Friday that employers had continued to demand cuts to existing sick pay entitlements, an issue on which they were not ready to negotiate.
"The employers must finally realise that no deal can be struck with IG Metall that is to the detriment of those workers who fall ill," IG Metall deputy chairman Walter Riester told journalists.
Dieter Hundt, chief negotiator for the Gesamtmetall metal and engineering employers federation, attacked trade union leaders for showing "no willingness for agreement".

Riester warned that unless another region could now put together a possible pilot agreement, the main 1997 wage round due to start for the 3.5 million workers in the sector in January could be "really dramatic".

Baden-Wuertemberg -- home to Daimler-Benz AG and its vehicle-making Mercedes Benz unit -- was the first region to attempt to find a solution to the dispute after national talks between the two sides broke down last month.

Daimler has been one of the main targets of protests involving hundreds of thousands of engineering workers after it tried to impose a new law cutting sick pay from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
Daimler has since said it would postpone making the cuts pending wider agreement in the industry.

IG Metall's Riester said there could now be a further attempt to seek a pilot deal in North-Rhine Westphalia, Germany's main steel area but that after that the issue would likely have to be settled within the main 1997 wage round.
Gesamtmetall's Hundt said employers had already gone "to the furthest extreme of what is possible" in their attempts to seek an agreement on sick pay.

He said employers had offered to continue paying full sick entitlements in return for employees losing 1.7 days of holiday for each three weeks of absence -- as opposed to the three days loss of holiday put forward in that earlier proposals.
The only area of agreement reached in the talks was in job protection measures that form part of IG Metall's 1997 wage demand.
The union agreed that in future companies suffering from a business downturn would be able to cut working hours with a proportional reduction in wages.
In return workers councils would seek a commitment from employers to prevent redundancies.
